nameStory: The Icelandic Scallop gets its name from the cold northern waters where it was first scientifically described, including those around Iceland. Like many Arctic and subarctic marine species, it reflects the chilly origins of this cold-water specialist that ventures south into New England's deeper, cooler waters.
description: The Icelandic Scallop is a marine bivalve mollusk that lives on the ocean floor in cold, deep waters. Like other scallops, it has two fan-shaped shells connected by a hinge, with distinctive radiating ridges that spread out like the ribs of a fan. This northern species is typically smaller than the sea scallops you might see at a seafood market, and it's rarely encountered except by deep-water fishermen or marine researchers. Its shells are usually whitish to pale brown with subtle color variations.

idTips.label: Fan-shaped shells
idTips.description: Two distinctive fan-shaped shells with prominent radiating ridges that feel rough to the touch, spreading outward from the hinge like ribs on a hand fan

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Smaller than common sea scallops, typically fitting comfortably in your palm with shells that feel surprisingly lightweight for their size

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Whitish to pale brown shells that may show subtle orange, pink, or yellow tints, often with a slightly chalky texture when dry

idTips.label: Radiating ridges
idTips.description: Prominent raised ribs running from the hinge to the shell edge that you can easily feel with your fingertip, creating a distinctive corrugated pattern

idTips.label: Habitat clue
idTips.description: Found in cold, deep waters rather than shallow tide pools, so any scallop shells washing up on New England beaches from deep water could be this species

habitat: Icelandic Scallops live in cold, deep waters off the New England coast, typically in depths where the water stays consistently chilly year-round. They prefer sandy or muddy ocean bottoms in the deeper parts of the Gulf of Maine and adjacent continental shelf waters. You're most likely to encounter their shells washed up on beaches after storms, or see them in deep-water fishing catches.

seasonality.spring: Shells may wash ashore during spring storms, when rough seas stir up deeper waters and bring deep-water species to the surface.
seasonality.summer: Living scallops are active in deep, cold waters offshore, but are rarely encountered by casual beachgoers during warm weather beach visits.
seasonality.fall: Storm season may bring more shells to shore as autumn weather creates larger waves that can transport deep-water shells to beaches.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms are most likely to wash shells ashore, as powerful waves reach deeper waters where these scallops live.

funFact: Unlike the sea scallops that "swim" by clapping their shells together and jet-propelling through the water, Icelandic Scallops are much more sedentary and prefer to stay put on the ocean floor, making them the homebodies of the scallop world.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other scallop species, especially bay scallops or young sea scallops. The key difference is habitat - if you find scallop shells on New England beaches that seem smaller than typical sea scallops but larger than bay scallops, and they washed up after a big storm, they could be Icelandic Scallops from deeper waters.
contextualKnowledge: Don't expect to find these scallops in your local seafood market - they're not commercially harvested like the common sea scallops. The few that are encountered in New England waters represent the southern edge of their range, as they're much more common in the colder waters of eastern Canada and the Arctic.
compareHints: Since this is the only Chlamys species regularly found in New England waters, compare it to other local scallops in the Pectinidae family. It's smaller than the common sea scallop but has more prominent radiating ridges, and unlike bay scallops, it comes from deep, cold water rather than shallow coastal bays.
